title: Revelation 9:1–12
context: The fifth trumpet opens the abyss, and smoke releases locust-like creatures that torment for five months those who lack God’s seal. Their king is the angel of the abyss, Abaddon or Apollyon. This is the first woe.

verses.text: The fifth angel sounded, and I saw a star from the sky which had fallen to the earth. The key to the pit of the abyss was given to him.
verses.arminianNotes: A fallen star receives the key to the abyss. Many take the star as an angel, possibly Satan; the key is given, so his power is permitted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the key was given: even the powers of darkness act only under God’s permission.

verses.text: He opened the pit of the abyss, and smoke went up out of the pit, like the smoke from a burning furnace. The sun and the air were darkened because of the smoke from the pit.
verses.arminianNotes: Smoke darkens the sun and air.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see spiritual darkness released as judgment.

verses.text: Then out of the smoke came locusts on the earth, and power was given to them, as the scorpions of the earth have power.
verses.arminianNotes: Locusts recall Joel and the eighth plague. Interpreters read them as demonic forces, invading armies, or symbols of spiritual torment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers commonly see demonic powers permitted to afflict unbelievers.

verses.text: They were told that they should not hurt the grass of the earth, neither any green thing, neither any tree, but only those people who don’t have God’s seal on their foreheads.
verses.arminianNotes: The locusts may harm only those without God’s seal. Arminian readers see God protecting his own.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the seal of chapter 7 at work: God’s people are protected from this spiritual torment.

verses.text: They were given power, not to kill them, but to torment them for five months. Their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it strikes a person.
verses.arminianNotes: They may torment but not kill, for five months, a limited time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see judgment restrained and limited.

verses.text: In those days people will seek death, and will in no way find it. They will desire to die, and death will flee from them.
verses.arminianNotes: People seek death and cannot find it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the misery of life under judgment without God.

verses.text: The shapes of the locusts were like horses prepared for war. On their heads were something like golden crowns, and their faces were like people’s faces.
verses.arminianNotes: The locusts look like war horses with crowns and human faces.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a picture of terrifying power that imitates authority.

verses.text: They had hair like women’s hair, and their teeth were like those of lions.
verses.arminianNotes: Hair like women’s and teeth like lions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see deceptive attraction joined with ferocity.

verses.text: They had breastplates like breastplates of iron. The sound of their wings was like the sound of many chariots and horses rushing to war.
verses.arminianNotes: Iron breastplates and the roar of chariots.

verses.text: They have tails like those of scorpions, with stingers. In their tails they have power to harm men for five months.
verses.arminianNotes: Stinging tails, with power limited to five months.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note again the limit.

verses.text: They have over them as king the angel of the abyss. His name in Hebrew is “Abaddon”, but in Greek, he has the name “Apollyon”.
verses.arminianNotes: Their king is Abaddon or Apollyon, meaning Destruction or Destroyer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Satan as the destroyer, in contrast to Christ the Savior.

verses.text: The first woe is past. Behold, there are still two woes coming after this.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the progression toward the end.
